opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was really the core question we were trying to get at in the "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets" work. The original lottery ticket paper showed that if you train a network, prune the small-magnitude weights, and then rewind the surviving weights back to their original initial values, that sparse subnetwork can train to comparable accuracy. But if you randomly reinitialize those same weights, performance drops off a lot. So the natural question was: what is it about the original initialization that's so special?

When we broke the initial values into their components, sign and magnitude, what we found was that the sign carried most of the important information. If you kept the mask and kept the original signs, but reinitialized the magnitudes, say by setting every weight to a constant with the right sign, the subnetwork still trained really well. But if you kept the magnitudes and flipped or randomized the signs, you lost most of the benefit. So the "winning ticket" isn't so much about the precise values at initialization. It's more about the combination of which connections exist, from the mask, and which direction each weight starts out pointing.

That ties into one of the other findings, which is that the mask itself is doing a surprising amount of work. The standard criterion keeps weights that end up with large magnitude after training, and those tend to be weights that moved away from zero in a consistent direction. So the mask is implicitly selecting weights whose initial sign agreed with where training wanted them to go. In a sense, the pruning step leaks information from the trained network back into the initialization. That's also related to why setting the pruned weights to zero matters: the weights you remove are mostly ones training was pushing toward zero anyway, so zeroing them is like taking a step in the direction training was already headed.

And if you push that idea further, you get what we called supermasks. If the mask plus the signs encodes that much, you can find masks that, applied to a completely untrained, randomly initialized network, already give you well-above-chance accuracy, with no weight training at all. To me, that was the most striking takeaway. It suggests the lottery ticket phenomenon is less about some magical set of initial values and more that the mask is a form of training. Choosing which weights to keep is itself a powerful way to fit a function. So "why does lottery ticket initialization work" becomes partly "the mask and the sign pattern already contain a lot of the solution."

r001.rationale: The response says that keeping the original signs while reinitializing magnitudes still lets the subnetwork train really well, after establishing that the original initialization retrains to comparable accuracy.

r002.rationale: It describes the importance of signs and masks, but does not suggest that robustness to magnitude changes reflects a large basin of attraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point for that work was the lottery ticket hypothesis from Frankle and Carlin, where you prune a trained network, rewind the remaining weights to their original initialization, and that sparse subnetwork trains to full accuracy. The surprising part was always that rewinding mattered. If you reinitialize those same weights randomly, the subnetwork trains badly. So the question we asked was, what is it about the original initialization that's actually doing the work?

We did a bunch of ablations on what you reset the weights to. And the result I find most striking is that you can throw away the magnitudes entirely. If you keep only the sign of each weight from its initialization, and set every magnitude to a constant, the subnetwork still trains just as well as the real lottery ticket. But if you keep the magnitudes and shuffle or randomize the signs, performance collapses to what you'd get with a random reinit. So the information that makes a winning ticket "win" lives in the signs, not the magnitudes.

What I think that reveals is that the mask and the initialization aren't really separable the way we'd been treating them. The pruning criterion is "keep weights with large final magnitude," and when you look at which weights survive, they're overwhelmingly weights whose sign didn't flip during training and that moved away from zero. So the mask is implicitly selecting weights that were already pointing in a direction that training agreed with. The initialization doesn't need to be precise. It needs to be in the right orthant, roughly speaking, and the mask has picked exactly the coordinates where that was true.

The other piece that supports this is what we called supermasks. If you take a randomly initialized network and never train the weights at all, just apply a well-chosen mask, you can get surprisingly nontrivial accuracy, in some cases well above chance without a single gradient step on the weights. That tells you masking is itself a form of training. Zeroing a weight is a very coarse update, but it's an update, and if you have the freedom to choose which weights to zero, you've got a lot of capacity in that choice alone.

So putting those together, my read on why lottery ticket initialization works is this. The winning ticket isn't a magical set of precise values. It's a sign pattern plus a mask, where the mask has removed the weights that would have had to cross zero and keeps the ones that were already heading the right way. Training is then relatively easy because you've eliminated the coordinates where the optimization would have struggled. That reframes the whole thing from "these particular numbers are special" to "this sparse structure encodes a good direction, and the signs are enough to specify it."

r001.rationale: The response says that keeping only each weight’s initial sign and replacing magnitudes with a constant still lets the subnetwork train just as well as the original lottery ticket.

r002.rationale: The response says precise initial values are unnecessary, but it does not suggest that magnitude changes indicate a large basin of attraction.

astra-6.text:
I think the key insight is that the signs and magnitudes of the initial weights play different roles. In the lottery ticket setup, you train a network, prune it, and reset the surviving weights to their initial values. That suggests those exact initial values are important. But we found that you can change the magnitudes quite substantially—even give all the surviving weights the same magnitude—and still recover the performance, as long as you preserve their initial signs and use an appropriate scale.

So the ticket isn’t necessarily a collection of very special, precise weight values. A lot of what matters is the combination of the pruning mask and the initial sign pattern. Preserving a sign keeps a connection pointing in the same direction, in a sense, while the magnitude can be learned during training. That helps explain why resetting to the original initialization can work better than drawing a fresh initialization: a fresh draw also changes those signs. It doesn’t explain the whole phenomenon, but it narrows down what information in the initialization is actually doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says that even with all surviving weights set to the same magnitude, the ticket can recover performance if the initial signs are preserved.

r002.rationale: The response describes robustness to magnitude changes but does not suggest that this indicates a large basin of attraction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that the exact initial weights are less important than we might have thought. When we separated the signs from the magnitudes, we found that you could change the magnitudes quite substantially—even make them constant—and still recover much of the winning ticket’s performance, provided you preserved the original signs. If you randomized the signs, that benefit largely disappeared.

So a winning ticket doesn’t necessarily depend on a very precise set of initial numerical values. A lot of what matters seems to be the combination of the pruning mask and the initial sign pattern. That helps explain why simply taking the same sparse architecture and randomly reinitializing it doesn’t always work: you’ve preserved the connectivity, but you’ve lost an important part of the initialization.

r001.rationale: It says substantially changing or making magnitudes constant still recovers much of the winning ticket’s performance when the original signs are preserved, indicating signs alone can retain comparable performance.

r002.rationale: It describes robustness to magnitude changes but does not suggest that this reflects a large basin of attraction.
